sections.overview: The Common Starling is a medium-sized, adaptable songbird native across much of Europe and temperate Asia. It moves between open feeding grounds and sheltered roosts, and often nests in cavities in trees or buildings. Its seasonal plumage, varied calls and large coordinated flocks make it conspicuous, while its ecological effects depend strongly on whether it lives within or beyond its native range.
sections.identification: Adults of both sexes are about 20–23 cm long and weigh 60–96 g. The consulted reference does not provide a dependable wingspan, height or body-width value for this species. Adults have a compact, dark body, short tail, pointed wings and a slender bill. The apparent blackness is broken by green, blue and purple iridescence: ordered melanosomes beneath a thin keratin layer in feather barbules produce structural colour whose hue changes with illumination and viewing angle. After the annual moult, fresh feathers carry pale tips that create conspicuous winter spots; abrasion gradually removes the tips towards spring, exposing the darker glossy feather. The bill is dark in winter and becomes yellow as breeding approaches. In breeding condition, the lower bill base is usually blue-grey in males and pink in females. A late-winter bird can therefore show both residual white spots and a yellow bill.
sections.habitat: Starlings use open country with short vegetation, including pasture, lawns, parks and cultivated fields, where the ground is accessible for probing. Trees, reedbeds and buildings provide night roosts; nest sites are cavities such as old woodpecker holes, tree hollows, nest boxes and gaps in structures. Their broad use of human-shaped landscapes helps explain successful establishment in several introduced regions, but does not make every introduced population equally damaging.
sections.diet: The diet shifts with season and opportunity. During much of the breeding season, adults search soil for invertebrates such as beetle larvae and other prey, which also provide protein for growing chicks; in other periods they take fruit, seeds and other available foods. A characteristic feeding sequence is to insert the closed bill into turf or soft soil, then force it open to widen the gap and expose hidden prey. This probing-and-gaping action reaches food beneath the surface, unlike simple picking from foliage.
sections.behavior: They forage in loose groups and gather in larger flocks at communal roosts, especially outside the breeding season. Before settling, flocks may wheel in dense aerial displays called murmurations. Measurements and models of starling flocks show that birds adjust direction and speed in response to nearby flockmates; local reactions can spread through the group, so no central leader is needed. Rapid turns propagate as birds respond to nearby flockmates and predators. Starlings also produce whistles, rattles and imitations within their vocal repertoire.
sections.reproduction: Starlings nest in cavities, where the male begins a nest of grasses and other material and the female helps finish it. A clutch usually contains three to six eggs; both parents incubate, and both feed the helpless hatchlings. Chicks remain in the nest for roughly three weeks before fledging, then continue to depend on adults while learning to forage. Some populations can raise a second brood when conditions allow. Nest cavities are a limiting resource in many landscapes, so competition for them can be intense.
sections.ecology: Within its native range, the starling consumes soil invertebrates and fruit and also supplies prey to predators. Its probing can affect the availability of pasture invertebrates, while large feeding flocks may concentrate pressure on particular fields. In North America, where it was introduced, competition for nest cavities can displace native cavity-nesting birds; a 2003 analysis of 27 native North American cavity-nesting species detected few population declines potentially attributable to starlings. The balance of effects is therefore local and evidence-dependent, rather than a universal property of the species.
sections.conservation: Global assessments classify the Common Starling as Least Concern because of its very large range and population. That category masks substantial regional differences. In the UK, the species is Red-listed: the British Trust for Ornithology reports a 61% decline in the breeding population from 1995 to 2024, and links concern to losses in pastoral farmland and reduced access to food. In North America and parts of Australasia it is introduced and can compete for nest cavities or cause agricultural problems, leading to local control policies. Conservation status and management therefore need a stated geography; a global category does not describe the condition of every regional population.
